name: Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy
summary: A load-related overuse tendinopathy of the main body of the Achilles tendon, 2–6 cm above the heel, causing pain and stiffness with running and jumping. It is managed with progressive calf and tendon loading.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Months, not weeks: 12-week loading blocks improved symptoms in RCTs, and full recovery can take up to a year

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based graded return to running and jumping after a loading block; recurrence is common during the return phase

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Localised mid-portion thickening and tenderness; arc sign (pooled Sp 88%, Sn 42%) and Royal London Hospital test (+LR 3.84)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed to make the diagnosis; ultrasound or MRI if a tear or other pathology is suspected

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Active adults; mean age about 50 in the trials reviewed

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 1.85 per 1000 patients registered with Dutch GPs; a sport link was recorded in only 35% of cases

overview:
Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy is a load-related overuse condition of the main body of the Achilles tendon. The painful, thickened area usually lies 2–6 cm above the calcaneal insertion (the usual anatomical definition). It causes pain and stiffness with running, jumping and sometimes walking, and it is not a tear: the tendon stays in continuity. It is a common overuse injury in athletes who run and jump [r1]. It also affects non-athletes: in Dutch primary care only 35% of cases had a recorded link to sport [r2].

The best-supported treatment is progressive calf and tendon loading. In network meta-analyses, active treatments (mainly exercise) were better than a wait-and-see approach, but the certainty of the evidence was low and no one loading protocol or add-on treatment was clearly superior [r3,r4]. Recovery is slow. It can take up to a year, and recurrence is common, especially while returning to sport [r1].

epidemiology.text: In a Dutch primary-care cohort of 57,725 registered patients, the incidence of mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy diagnosed by a GP was 1.85 per 1000 per year, rising to 2.35 per 1000 in adults aged 21–60. A relationship with sport was recorded in 35% of cases, and the authors noted that the true incidence may be higher [r2]. A systematic review of clinical risk factors found only limited evidence from cohort studies, all at high risk of bias. Several factors that clinicians often suspect, including being overweight, static foot posture and physical activity level, were not associated with Achilles tendinopathy in that review [r5].

intrinsic: Prior lower-limb tendinopathy or fracture (limited evidence) [r5]
Decreased isokinetic plantar flexor strength (limited evidence; potentially modifiable) [r5]
Gait features: decreased forward progression of propulsion and more lateral foot roll-over at forefoot flat (limited evidence) [r5]
Kidney impairment (creatinine clearance below 60 mL/min) in heart-transplant recipients (limited evidence from a specific population) [r5]
Older age and diabetes or renal failure raise the risk of fluoroquinolone-associated tendinopathy [r6]
extrinsic: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics, including ofloxacin (limited evidence; modifiable by the prescriber) [r5,r6]
Rapid increases in running or jumping volume, intensity, hills or speed work, or a change of footwear or surface (common clinical observation; not established by the sources reviewed)

mechanism.summary: There is no single injury moment. In running, the Achilles tendon is stretched as the ankle dorsiflexes over the planted foot, then recoils as the calf drives the ankle into plantarflexion at toe-off. Each cycle loads the tendon several times body weight, and thousands of cycles are repeated per run. When load rises faster than the tendon's capacity, or recovery between sessions is too short, the mid-portion matrix cannot keep up and becomes painful and thickened (general biomechanics; no single source).
sequence: Foot contact: the foot lands and the tibia advances over it, so the ankle dorsiflexes while the gastrocnemius and soleus work eccentrically.
Mid-stance: the Achilles lengthens and stores elastic energy while the knee and hip flex under the body's weight.
Late stance to toe-off: the knee and hip extend and the calf contracts concentrically, driving the ankle into rapid plantarflexion as the tendon recoils.
Tensile load through the tendon peaks around push-off. It is highest in running, hills, sprinting and jumping.
Repeated sessions: with enough recovery and a gradual build-up, the tendon adapts; with a sudden rise in volume or intensity, or too little recovery, load exceeds capacity.
The mid-portion responds with tenocyte activation, matrix swelling and, if overload continues, collagen disorganisation and new vessels [r7,r8].
The tendon thickens into a tender, fusiform swelling 2–6 cm above the heel, which is painful with load and stiff after rest, but it remains in continuity.

variants.name: Reactive episode after a load spike
variants.description: A sudden increase in training, such as a new hill program, speed work, a pre-season jump in volume or a return from a break, can produce a swollen, sensitive tendon within days to weeks [r7].

variants.name: Long-standing degenerative tendinopathy
variants.description: Months to years of symptoms, with a nodular, thickened tendon and weaker calf. It responds more slowly [r7,r9].

variants.name: Fluoroquinolone-associated tendinopathy
variants.description: Tendon pain, with a risk of rupture, can follow fluoroquinolone antibiotics, especially in older people and in those with diabetes or renal failure. Management includes stopping the drug [r6].

variants.name: Non-athletic presentation
variants.description: A sport link was recorded in only 35% of primary-care cases, so do not exclude the diagnosis in people who do not run or play sport [r2].

anatomy.text: The Achilles is the common tendon of the gastrocnemius (medial and lateral heads) and soleus. It forms in the distal calf, and its fibres twist as they descend to the posterior calcaneal tuberosity. It is surrounded by a paratenon rather than a synovial sheath. The mid-portion, roughly 2–6 cm proximal to the insertion, is the usual site of tendinopathy. It is commonly described as a region of relatively poor blood supply, but the sources reviewed here do not quantify this. The tendon works as a spring: it stores elastic energy as the ankle dorsiflexes and returns it at push-off.

structures.name: Achilles tendon (mid-portion)
structures.role: Transmits triceps surae force to the calcaneus and stores and returns elastic energy in walking, running and jumping

structures.name: Gastrocnemius (medial and lateral heads)
structures.role: Biarticular plantarflexor and knee flexor; contributes most to fast, powerful push-off with the knee extended

structures.name: Soleus
structures.role: Monoarticular plantarflexor; the main stance-phase ankle stabiliser and the dominant plantarflexor with the knee bent

structures.name: Paratenon
structures.role: Gliding layer around the tendon; can be involved alongside the tendon in some presentations

structures.name: Plantaris tendon
structures.role: Thin tendon running along the medial side of the Achilles; sometimes implicated in medial mid-portion pain

structures.name: Retrocalcaneal bursa and Kager's fat pad
structures.role: Cushion and glide space at the insertion; relevant to the differential with insertional tendinopathy

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy is a failure of the tendon to adapt to load, not a rupture. The continuum model describes a reactive response to acute overload, then attempted repair with matrix disorganisation (disrepair), and in some people a degenerative state with areas of cell death. The stages overlap and can move in either direction [r7]. Histological studies of Achilles tendinopathy report more tenocytes and glycosaminoglycan in the ground substance, disorganised and fragmented collagen, and neovascularisation [r8].

Staging by structure alone is too simple for what is primarily a pain condition: the interplay between structure, pain and function is not fully understood [r10]. After 12 weeks of eccentric or heavy slow resistance training, tendon thickness and neovascularisation fell as symptoms improved, although the study did not show that structural change drives the clinical gain [r11].

structures.name: Achilles tendon mid-portion
structures.effect: Focal thickening, disorganised and fragmented collagen, more tenocytes and ground substance, and neovascularisation. The tendon stays in continuity [r7,r8]

structures.name: Paratenon
structures.effect: May be thickened or adherent in some presentations. A pure paratenon problem is not separated from tendinopathy in the sources reviewed.

structures.name: Tendon structure and symptoms
structures.effect: The interplay between structure, pain and function is not fully understood [r10], so the diagnosis rests on history and examination and imaging is not needed to make it (clinical convention).

muscles.name: Triceps surae (gastrocnemius and soleus)
muscles.effect: Weakness and reduced endurance. In the original eccentric-training series the injured calf had lower eccentric and concentric strength than the uninjured side [r12]. Decreased plantar flexor strength is a limited-evidence risk factor [r5].

muscles.name: Calf function and fear of movement
muscles.effect: In a 5-year follow-up, higher kinesiophobia was moderately correlated (r = -0.590) with poorer recovery of heel-rise work [r9].

muscles.name: Kinetic chain (hip, foot, trunk)
muscles.effect: Gait features such as reduced forward propulsion were limited-evidence risk factors. Capacity deficits further up the chain shift load to the Achilles, but trial evidence that treating them changes outcomes was not found [r5].

cellular.description: Tenocytes activate and produce proteoglycan, so the matrix takes up water and the tendon thickens. This short-term adaptive response can reverse with reduced load [r7].
More cells and protein production in an attempt at repair, with collagen disorganisation and new vessels [r7,r8].
Areas of cell death and disorganised matrix, with limited capacity to reverse. Pain and function can still improve with loading [r7,r10].
With eccentric or heavy slow resistance training, symptoms improved and tendon thickness and neovascularisation fell, and the gains were maintained at 52 weeks [r11].

systems.effect: Tendinopathy is primarily a pain condition, and how structure, pain and function relate is not fully understood [r10]. A single bout of isometric calf contractions reduced pain during a functional load test by roughly half in a small crossover pilot, so pain can change rapidly without any structural change [r13].
Gait pattern and plantar flexor strength relate to risk, so assess calf capacity, foot mechanics and training load together [r5].
Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are associated with tendinopathy and rupture, particularly in older people and in diabetes or renal failure. Ask about recent antibiotic courses [r6,r5].
Kinesiophobia was related to poorer functional recovery after exercise treatment, which is why a pain-monitoring model and clear education are recommended [r9].

grading.system: Tendinopathy continuum (Cook and Purdam): a structural staging model, to be used alongside pain and function [r7,r10]

grades.description: Short-term adaptive response to acute overload: swelling and a thickened but otherwise intact tendon, with pain that is higher with load [r7].
grades.prognosis: Often settles with load adjustment followed by gradual re-exposure

grades.description: Attempted repair with more matrix disorganisation and increased vascularity if overload continues [r7].
grades.prognosis: Responds to progressive loading; some change can partly reverse

grades.description: Areas of cell death and disorganised matrix, usually a thickened or nodular tendon [r7].
grades.prognosis: Structure rarely normalises, but capacity can be rebuilt and pain reduced; recovery is usually slower

timeframes.summary: The continuum describes load history, not a calendar, so the stage durations below are illustrative and overlap. In trials, clinically meaningful gains were assessed after 12 weeks of loading, and full recovery can take up to a year [r11,r1].

healing.description: Tenocyte activation and matrix swelling after a load spike; settles with load adjustment [r7]
Attempted repair with matrix disorganisation and neovascularisation if overload continues [r7]
Cell death and disorganised matrix in long-standing overload; limited reversibility, although pain can still improve [r7]
A 12-week block of eccentric or heavy slow resistance training improved symptoms; gains were maintained at 52 weeks [r11]

milestones.label: Short-term pain relief from isometric holds
milestones.note: Pain during a functional load test fell by about half immediately after isometric calf holds in a small crossover pilot (n = 11) [r13]

milestones.label: Continued running and jumping with pain monitoring
milestones.note: In an RCT (n = 38) patients who kept running and jumping within a pain-monitoring model improved as much as those who rested for the first 6 weeks [r14]

milestones.label: 12-week loading block complete
milestones.note: Both eccentric and heavy slow resistance training improved VISA-A and pain at 12 weeks [r11]

milestones.label: Minimum exercise trial before other treatments
milestones.note: Exercise for at least 3 months is recommended before other options are considered [r1]

milestones.label: Recovery for many people
milestones.note: Full recovery can take up to a year, and improvements were maintained at 52 weeks in an RCT [r1,r11]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based. Typically 3–6 months or longer after starting a loading program for an established tendinopathy (a clinical range), and recovery can take up to a year. Recurrence is common during the return-to-sport (RTS) phase, so progress running and jumping load in steps [r1].

symptoms: Gradual onset of Achilles pain 2–6 cm above the heel during or after running, jumping or hill walking
Morning stiffness or pain with the first steps, easing with warm-up and often returning later or the next day
Pain with stairs, uphill walking or rising onto the toes
Tenderness and swelling in the mid-tendon, sometimes with a palpable lump
A reduced ability to run, hop or push off at the usual intensity
signs: Fusiform thickening or a nodule in the mid-portion, tender to pinch palpation
Arc sign: the swelling moves with the tendon as the ankle moves from dorsiflexion to plantarflexion
Pain or fewer repetitions on single-leg heel raise, with a lower calf endurance than the other side
Pain on hopping or jumping that matches the patient's complaint
Normal passive ankle range, apart from mild stiffness; a Thompson test that shows plantarflexion on calf squeeze

subjective: Location and behaviour of pain: mid-tendon, load-related, morning stiffness, warm-up pattern
Training history: volume, intensity, hills, speed work, surface and footwear in the past 4–6 weeks, and any recent break or change
Previous Achilles or other tendon problems, and prior treatment including injections
Recent fluoroquinolone antibiotics, corticosteroid exposure, diabetes, kidney disease [r5,r6]
Sudden event, pop or loss of push-off (rupture), and calf swelling or warmth (DVT)
Patient goals, sport demands and fear of movement; the Victorian Institute of Sport Assessment (VISA-A) as a baseline [r15]
observation: Swelling or fusiform thickening of the mid-tendon, compared with the other side
Foot posture, heel alignment and gait or running pattern (limited-evidence risk features) [r5]
palpation: Pinch palpation across the mid-portion 2–6 cm above the insertion to find the tender, thickened segment
Check the insertion and retrocalcaneal area to separate insertional pain
Palpate for a gap (rupture) and for medial plantaris-region tenderness
rangeOfMotion: Passive ankle dorsiflexion with the knee straight and bent (calf extensibility), compared with the other side
Subtalar and first-ray range, as part of the kinetic-chain screen
Note that terminal dorsiflexion often stresses the tendon but is not a diagnostic test
strength: Single-leg heel-rise endurance (number of repetitions and height, ideally measured as work) compared with the other side [r9]
Isometric plantarflexion strength with the knee straight and bent
Hip extensor and abductor strength, as part of the chain
functional: Single-leg hop for distance and repeated hopping: pain response and symmetry
Running assessment when appropriate: cadence, foot strike, calf use and trunk control

specialTests.name: Arc sign
specialTests.purpose: Locate pain and swelling to the tendon rather than the paratenon or surrounding tissue
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the thickened area of the mid-portion with the ankle in neutral. Move the ankle actively between dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.
specialTests.positive: The swelling and tenderness move with the tendon as the ankle moves.

specialTests.name: Royal London Hospital test
specialTests.purpose: Distinguish tenderness within the tendon from tenderness in the paratenon
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the tender area with the ankle in plantarflexion (tendon slack), then in dorsiflexion (tendon under tension).
specialTests.positive: Tenderness is significantly reduced or disappears when the tendon is under tension.

specialTests.name: Palpation for localised tendon tenderness
specialTests.procedure: Pinch the tendon between thumb and index finger along its length and compare sides.
specialTests.positive: Focal tenderness in the mid-portion that reproduces the patient's pain.

specialTests.name: Thompson (calf squeeze) test
specialTests.purpose: Exclude a complete Achilles rupture before loading (accuracy is discussed on the rupture page)
specialTests.procedure: With the patient prone and the foot over the end of the couch, squeeze the calf.
specialTests.positive: No plantarflexion on squeeze suggests rupture.

specialTests.name: Single-leg heel-rise test
specialTests.purpose: Calf capacity: a baseline and progress measure rather than a diagnostic test
specialTests.procedure: Single-leg heel raises to a consistent height and tempo until fatigue or pain stops the set, compared with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Fewer repetitions, lower height or pain compared with the other side.

outcomeMeasures.name: VISA-A questionnaire
outcomeMeasures.use: Eight-item severity index (pain, function, sport) scored 0–100; mean 64 in non-surgical patients and above 96 in controls in the original study. It is not designed to be diagnostic [r15]. A 12-point change was used as the minimal clinically important difference in a large RCT [r18]

outcomeMeasures.name: Numeric pain rating during a functional load test
outcomeMeasures.use: Pain during single-leg heel rise or hop, used to guide the pain-monitoring model and as an immediate-response measure [r13,r14]

outcomeMeasures.name: Single-leg heel-rise endurance or work
outcomeMeasures.use: Calf capacity and recovery of function [r9]

outcomeMeasures.name: Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia
outcomeMeasures.use: Screens fear of movement, which was related to poorer recovery [r9]

imaging.indication: If the diagnosis is uncertain, a partial or complete tear is suspected, or the patient fails to respond to well-delivered loading
imaging.findings: Focal thickening and disorganised, hypoechoic tendon; neovascularisation on Doppler. These findings reduced after 12 weeks of loading [r11]

imaging.indication: Atypical presentation, suspected partial tear, or pre-surgical planning
imaging.findings: Tendon thickening and intratendinous signal change; also shows paratenon, bursa and other posterior ankle pathology

imaging.indication: Insertional or posterior heel pain, or suspected calcification or bony spur
imaging.findings: Insertional spur or calcification, more relevant to insertional than to mid-portion disease

differentials.name: Partial or complete Achilles rupture
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden pop, giving way and weak push-off. A palpable gap, a positive Thompson test and an abnormal resting foot position favour a complete tear.

differentials.name: Insertional Achilles tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Pain at the tendon-bone junction on the posterior heel, often with a Haglund prominence or retrocalcaneal bursitis. Pain is worse with end-range dorsiflexion and heel compression.

differentials.name: Medial gastrocnemius strain
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden onset during lunging or sprinting, with pain and tenderness in the muscle belly or musculotendinous junction rather than in the tendon.

differentials.name: Soleus strain
differentials.distinguishing: Deeper calf pain that is worse with the knee bent, often with a more gradual onset in runners.

differentials.name: Posterior ankle impingement
differentials.distinguishing: Deep posterior ankle pain with forced plantarflexion, often involving an os trigonum or the flexor hallucis longus; the tendon itself is not thickened.

differentials.name: Plantaris tendon involvement or paratenonitis
differentials.distinguishing: Medial mid-portion pain or crepitus. Imaging or specialist assessment is often needed to separate it from tendinopathy.

differentials.name: Retrocalcaneal bursitis
differentials.distinguishing: Tenderness anterior to the tendon at its insertion, with swelling on both sides of the tendon just above the heel.

redFlags: Sudden pop or a blow to the back of the leg, immediate loss of push-off, a palpable gap or a positive Thompson test: suspect Achilles rupture. Do not load the tendon, protect the ankle in plantarflexion and arrange urgent orthopaedic review (ideally within 48 hours).

Unilateral calf swelling, warmth, tenderness or pitting oedema, especially after recent immobilisation, surgery or long travel: suspect deep vein thrombosis. Arrange same-day medical assessment, and refer urgently if there is breathlessness or chest pain (pulmonary embolism).
Recent or current fluoroquinolone antibiotic use with new Achilles pain: ask the patient to contact the prescriber the same day to review the drug, and avoid heavy tendon loading until reviewed [r6].
Recent corticosteroid injection around the Achilles: avoid heavy or ballistic loading and refer for medical advice if there is sudden pain or weakness (rupture risk is a recognised clinical concern).

Bilateral or multi-site tendon pain with morning stiffness, other joint pain, psoriasis, bowel or eye symptoms, or lumps on several tendons: suggest inflammatory arthritis or a metabolic cause and refer for medical review.
Constant night pain, fever, or a hot, red, swollen heel or tendon: suspect infection or an inflammatory process and arrange urgent medical review.

management.principles: Treat mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy as a load-capacity problem. Educate the patient, adjust tendon load and build capacity with a progressive calf and tendon-loading program, as exercise is the intervention with the highest level of evidence and should be tried for at least 3 months before other options [r1,r3]. Wait-and-see (rest alone) performed worse than active treatment [r3,r4]. A pain-monitoring model lets many athletes keep running and jumping within limits while they load the tendon [r14,r9]. Evidence for any add-on treatment is limited. The full text of the 2018 APTA Orthopaedic Section clinical practice guideline [r19] could not be accessed for this page, so its individual recommendation grades are not reproduced here; use it alongside this page.

medical.name: Review of fluoroquinolone antibiotic use
medical.description: If the patient is taking or has recently taken a fluoroquinolone, the prescriber should review the drug. Management of fluoroquinolone-associated tendinopathy includes immediate discontinuation, then rest from heavy loading and graded exercise [r6,r5].

medical.name: Simple analgesia or short-course oral or topical NSAIDs
medical.description: May ease pain enough to allow loading. Evidence that anti-inflammatory drugs change the long-term course of the tendinopathy was not identified in the sources reviewed.

medical.name: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection
medical.description: In a participant-blinded RCT of 240 adults with chronic mid-portion tendinopathy, a single PRP injection did not improve VISA-A at 6 months compared with a sham injection (54.4 vs 53.4; adjusted difference -2.7, 95% CI -8.8 to 3.3). The authors concluded the findings do not support its use [r18].

medical.name: High-volume image-guided injection, with or without corticosteroid
medical.description: Specialist-delivered, after failed loading. In a network meta-analysis, high-volume injection with corticosteroid added to eccentric exercise improved VISA-A more than eccentric exercise alone in the short term (SMD 1.08, 95% CI 0.58–1.58) and the longer term (SMD 0.53, 95% CI 0.05–1.02). This came from a small number of trials, so the result should be interpreted cautiously [r4].

medical.name: Direct intratendinous corticosteroid injection
medical.description: Many clinicians avoid injecting corticosteroid into or around a loaded Achilles because of the risk of weakening the tendon. The rupture risk was not quantified in the sources reviewed.

medical.name: Surgical referral
medical.description: For patients who have not improved after at least 3 months of well-delivered exercise, and more often after 6 months, referral to an orthopaedic or sports physician is reasonable. Exercise should come first [r1]. Surgical outcomes were not reviewed for this page.

physio.name: Education and load management using a pain-monitoring model
physio.description: Explain the load-capacity model and monitor pain during and after loading and the next morning. A common clinical convention is to accept pain up to about 5/10 during exercise provided it settles by the next day. In an RCT (n = 38), patients who continued running and jumping with a pain-monitoring model improved as much as those who rested for 6 weeks, with no negative effects shown [r14]. A 5-year follow-up recommends the model because fear of movement was related to worse recovery [r9].

physio.name: Progressive calf-muscle and Achilles loading program
physio.description: Exercise is the best-supported treatment. Active treatments, mainly exercise, were better than wait-and-see at 3 months, with no clinically relevant difference between active treatments. Certainty was very low to low because no trial was at low risk of bias [r3]. Eccentric exercise was better than wait-and-see in the longer term [r4]. Start with a calf-muscle exercise program because it is easy to prescribe, low cost and has few harms [r3].

physio.name: Heavy slow resistance (HSR) training
physio.description: In an RCT of 58 patients with chronic mid-portion tendinopathy, 12 weeks of HSR and eccentric training gave equally good, lasting clinical results at 52 weeks. HSR had better compliance (92% vs 78%) and tended to give greater satisfaction at 12 weeks (100% vs 80%; P = .052) [r11].

physio.name: Eccentric (Alfredson-type) heel-drop training
physio.description: In the original uncontrolled series, all 15 recreational athletes returned to running after 12 weeks, whereas the 15 who had conventional treatment all went on to surgery [r12]. In the later RCT eccentric training was no better than HSR [r11], and in a network meta-analysis it outperformed wait-and-see in the longer term [r4].

physio.name: Isometric calf holds for short-term pain relief
physio.description: In a randomised crossover pilot of 11 people, isometric plantarflexion holds gave an immediate mean pain reduction of 1.6 points with the knee straight and 1.3 points with the knee flexed to 80° during a functional load test, about 50% overall. No long-term benefit has been shown [r13].

physio.name: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) as an adjunct
physio.description: Added to eccentric exercise, ESWT gave better longer-term VISA-A results than eccentric exercise alone in a network meta-analysis (SMD 0.99, 95% CI 0.48–1.49). Use it after a loading program is under way, not instead of one [r4].

physio.name: Staged return-to-sport program
physio.description: Plan return to running and jumping in steps, with load criteria. Recovery can take up to a year, and recurrence is common during the return phase [r1].

physio.name: Heel lifts or cushioned footwear in the irritable phase
physio.description: A short-term strategy to reduce tendon strain while pain settles. Trial evidence was not identified in the sources reviewed.

physio.name: Passive treatment alone (massage, ultrasound, taping, stretching)
physio.description: These do not build tendon capacity. Use them only to make loading possible.

physio.name: Rest alone or wait-and-see
physio.description: Wait-and-see produced worse outcomes than eccentric exercise in the longer term, and every active treatment seemed superior at 3 months, although certainty was low [r3,r4].

education: The pain is a sign that the tendon's load has outgrown its capacity. The tendon is not torn, and capacity can be rebuilt.
Exercise is the main treatment. Improvement takes months rather than weeks, so stay with the program even when the pain eases.
You can usually keep moving. A little pain during exercise is acceptable if it settles by the next morning. If it is clearly worse the next day, drop the load a step.
A scan does not decide your outcome: structure and pain do not always match, so treatment is guided by how the tendon responds to load.
Tell any prescriber about your Achilles pain before taking fluoroquinolone antibiotics, and avoid steroid injections into the tendon.
Recurrence is common during the return to running and jumping, so build up gradually and keep up the calf strength work.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based: settle the tendon and keep it loaded, build calf strength with heavy slow resistance, add energy-storage (plyometric) work, then return to running and sport in steps. Move on when the criteria are met, not when a set number of weeks has passed. Dosages below are typical clinical ranges rather than prescriptions from a single trial. The 12-week eccentric or heavy slow resistance blocks in the trials are the evidence base [r11,r12]. A common clinical convention is to accept pain up to about 5/10 during exercise if it has settled by the next morning, following the pain-monitoring model [r14]. Recovery can take up to a year [r1].

stages.name: Settle the tendon & start loading
goals: Calm load-related pain and morning stiffness
Keep the calf working and prevent deconditioning
Remove load spikes without stopping all activity
Teach the load-capacity model and pain monitoring
precautions: Exclude rupture (Thompson test) and DVT before loading
Avoid complete rest and avoid steroid injection into the tendon
Keep pain at or below about 5/10 during exercise and settled by the next morning (clinical convention) [r14]

exercises.name: Isometric seated calf hold (knee bent)
exercises.dosage: 5 × 30–45 s at moderate to high effort, 1–2 times daily (typical clinical dosage)
exercises.cues: Push up through the forefoot and hold steady without bouncing. Pain should ease during the set [r13].

exercises.name: Isometric standing calf hold (knee straight)
exercises.dosage: 5 × 30–45 s at moderate effort, 1–2 times daily
exercises.cues: Hold the heel lifted at mid-range

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise (slow)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 15, 3 s up and 3 s down, daily
exercises.cues: Pause at the top and keep the weight on the big toe side

exercises.name: Glute bridge
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels and keep the ribs down

exercises.name: Low-impact conditioning (cycling or pool)
exercises.dosage: 20–30 min, 3 times per week below the pain threshold
exercises.cues: Maintain fitness while the tendon settles

progressionCriteria: Morning stiffness settling and pain during daily activity at or below about 3/10
Isometric holds completed without a next-day increase in pain
Able to perform 15 double-leg heel raises pain-free

stages.name: Build calf strength (heavy slow resistance)
goals: Progressively increase calf and Achilles load tolerance
Build hip and thigh strength alongside
Maintain a pain-monitored volume of walking and jogging
precautions: Increase load only when pain and stiffness the next morning are stable
Avoid sudden jumps in resistance or volume
Reduce one step if pain rises above about 5/10 or lingers into the next day (clinical convention)

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise (heavy, slow)
exercises.dosage: 3–4 × 6–15 with a 3 s up and 3 s down tempo, 3 times per week; add load as it becomes easy (typical clinical protocol)
exercises.cues: Full range from low heel to high on the forefoot

exercises.name: Seated (bent-knee) calf raise with load
exercises.cues: Targets the soleus. Use a dumbbell or machine load on the thigh.

exercises.name: Eccentric heel drop off a step
exercises.dosage: 3 × 15 on each leg with the knee straight and again with the knee bent, daily (Alfredson-type) if used [r12]
exercises.cues: Lift with both feet, lower slowly on the painful leg

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift
exercises.cues: Hinge at the hips with a long spine

progressionCriteria: Single-leg calf raises with added load, no more than mild next-day symptoms
Single-leg heel-rise endurance approaching that of the other side
Pain during activity usually 3/10 or less

stages.name: Energy storage & plyometrics
goals: Restore the spring-like stretch-shortening function of the tendon
Keep calf strength while adding speed
precautions: Introduce plyometrics only when single-leg heel-rise work and strength are close to the other side
Build the volume of ground contacts gradually and review after each session
Warm up the calf with slow calf raises before jumping

exercises.name: Double-leg pogo hops
exercises.cues: Stiff ankles, quick ground contact, quiet landing

exercises.name: Single-leg hop in place
exercises.cues: Land softly and keep the knee over the second toe

progressionCriteria: No next-day increase in pain or stiffness after plyometrics
Single-leg heel-rise and hop performance within about 10% of the other side (clinical convention)
VISA-A improving towards the range of healthy controls (above 96 in the original validation sample) [r15]

stages.name: Return to running & sport
goals: Graded return to running, then speed, hills and sport-specific work
Prevent recurrence in the return phase
precautions: Increase the volume first, then the intensity
Allow rest days between running sessions at first
Recurrence is common in this phase, so keep a calf strength program running alongside sport [r1]

exercises.name: Walk–run progression
exercises.dosage: Alternate short jog and walk intervals on non-consecutive days, increasing jog time as pain allows (typical clinical protocol)
exercises.cues: Monitor pain during and the next morning

exercises.name: Continuous running with gradual weekly progression
exercises.dosage: Increase total volume by a modest amount weekly, then add hills or speed one at a time
exercises.cues: Keep a cadence of short, quick steps

exercises.name: Sport-specific jumping, acceleration and change of direction
exercises.dosage: 2–3 sessions per week, building from controlled to unplanned

exercises.name: Heavy calf strength maintenance
exercises.cues: Keep this in for the long term

progressionCriteria: Completes the graded running program with no next-day increase in pain
Single-leg heel-rise endurance and hop performance symmetrical with the other side (clinical convention)
Tolerates sport-specific training at full intensity for a week
Patient is confident and understands how to monitor pain

criteria: Pain with daily activity and load tests is minimal, with no next-day increase after running or jumping (clinical convention)
Single-leg heel-rise endurance and hop tests symmetrical with the other side (typically 90% or better; clinical convention)
Completion of a graded running and jumping program without a flare [r1]
VISA-A score approaching the range of healthy controls [r15]
Confidence in loading the tendon and a clear plan for managing training load, including continued calf strength work
tests: Single-leg heel-rise endurance or work, compared with the other side
Single hop, repeated hop and drop-jump or counter-movement jump testing
Pain response to a loading test and the next morning

prognosis: Most people improve with exercise, but recovery is slow and recurrence is common. In a 5-year follow-up of 34 patients treated with exercise alone, 80% had fully recovered, 15% had a new occurrence of symptoms and 20% had continued symptoms, so this was a small case series, not a population estimate [r9]. In a trial of people with symptoms for more than 3 months, mean VISA-A in the sham arm was still 53.4 at 6 months, which shows that persistent symptoms are common [r18]. Recovery can take up to a year, and recurrence is most likely during the return-to-sport phase [r1].
prevention: Build running and jumping volume and intensity gradually, and change only one training variable at a time (common clinical advice; not tested in trials reviewed here).
Keep calf strength and endurance up with regular heavy calf work; reduced plantar flexor strength was a limited-evidence risk factor [r5].
Ask prescribers to consider alternatives to fluoroquinolone antibiotics in people with Achilles symptoms or other risk factors [r6,r5].
After an episode, keep the calf strength program going, because recurrence is common [r1].
clinicalPearls: Tendon pain that warms up and returns later, or with first steps in the morning, is the typical pattern. Constant or night pain needs another explanation.
The arc sign and Royal London test help to locate the pain in the tendon, but they miss many cases. A negative test does not rule out tendinopathy (pooled arc sign sensitivity 42%) [r16].
Always do a Thompson test before loading, and screen for recent fluoroquinolone and injection history [r6].
Load is the active ingredient. Choose the version of the program the patient will actually complete: HSR had higher compliance than eccentric training (92% vs 78%) [r11].
Teach the pain-monitoring rule in the first session, and re-check it each visit, because fear of movement predicts poorer recovery [r14,r9].
Do not promise a quick fix from an add-on. A single PRP injection was no better than sham at 6 months, and other add-ons rest on small trials [r18,r4].

forces.label: Calf pulls up: the tendon stretches and stores energy

captions.text: A runner increases weekly mileage. Every stride loads the Achilles tendon.
In stance the ankle dorsiflexes, and the calf pulls on the tendon like a stretching spring.
At toe-off the calf drives the ankle into plantarflexion as the tendon recoils.
Healthy tendons adapt when load rises gradually and recovery is long enough.
When volume rises faster than the tendon's capacity, load exceeds capacity.
There is no single injury moment: pain builds over weeks as the mid-portion fails to adapt.
Zooming into the right calf and Achilles, viewed from behind.

actions.text: Achilles tendon: a spring between calf and heel

captions.text: The Achilles joins the calf muscles to the heel bone and stores and returns energy with each step.
In stance the calf pulls up while the heel anchors the tendon, so the tendon lengthens.
At push-off it recoils and gives the energy back.
With repeated loading beyond its capacity, the tendon swells and pain appears with activity.
The pain and thickening centre on the mid-portion, 2–6 cm above the heel.
The collagen becomes disorganised and thick, with extra vessels. The tendon degenerates; it does not tear.
Scans show the change, but structure and pain do not always match, so diagnosis stays clinical.
Healthy tendon: tightly packed, aligned type I collagen with a few resident tenocytes.
Reactive: after a load spike, tenocytes activate and the matrix swells. This can reverse.
Disrepair: cells try to repair the tendon, the collagen becomes disorganised and new vessels appear.
Degenerative: areas of cell death and disorganised matrix remain, with limited capacity to reverse.
Progressive loading builds capacity. Symptoms improve as the tendon adapts.
